title: Computational-Statistical Tradeoffs at the Next-Token Prediction Barrier: Autoregressive and Imitation Learning under Misspecification (extended abstract)
authors: Dhruv Rohatgi, Adam Block, Audrey Huang, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Dylan J. Foster

Proceedings of Machine Learning Research vol 291:1–7, 2025                  38th Annual Conference on Learning Theory




Computational-Statistical Tradeoffs at the Next-Token Prediction Barrier
                 Autoregressive and Imitation Learning under Misspecification


 Dhruv Rohatgi                                                                              DROHATGI @ MIT. EDU
 MIT

 Adam Block                                                                    BLOCKADAM @ MICROSOFT. COM
 Microsoft Research

 Audrey Huang                                                                        AUDREYH 5@ ILLINOIS . EDU
 UIUC

 Akshay Krishnamurthy                                                            AKSHAYKR @ MICROSOFT. COM
 Microsoft Research

 Dylan J. Foster                                                             DYLANFOSTER @ MICROSOFT. COM
 Microsoft Research



 Editors: Nika Haghtalab and Ankur Moitra



                                                          Abstract
            Next-token prediction with the logarithmic loss is a cornerstone of autoregressive sequence
       modeling, but, in practice, suffers from error amplification, where errors in the model compound
       and generation quality degrades as sequence length H increases. From a theoretical perspective,
       this phenomenon should not appear in well-specified settings, and, indeed, a growing body of
       empirical work hypothesizes that misspecification, where the learner is not sufficiently expressive to
       represent the target distribution, may be the root cause. Under misspecification—where the goal is
       to learn as well as the best-in-class model up to a multiplicative approximation factor Capx ≥ 1—
       we confirm that Capx indeed grows with H for next-token prediction, lending theoretical support
       to this empirical hypothesis. We then ask whether this mode of error amplification is avoidable
       algorithmically, computationally, or information-theoretically, and uncover inherent computational-
       statistical tradeoffs.
            We show: (1) Information-theoretically, one can avoid error amplification and achieve Capx =
       O(1). (2) Next-token prediction can be made robust to achieve Capx = O(H),
                                                                               e      representing moderate
       error amplification, but this is an inherent barrier: any next-token prediction-style objective must
       suffer Capx = Ω(H). (3) For the natural testbed of autoregressive linear models, no computationally
                                                                                             1−Ω(1)
       efficient algorithm can achieve sub-polynomial approximation factor Capx = e(log H)          ; however,
       at least for binary token spaces, one can smoothly trade compute for statistical power and improve
       on Capx = Ω(H) in sub-exponential time. Our results have consequences in the more general setting
       of imitation learning, where the widely-used behavior cloning generalizes next-token prediction.1
       Keywords: Next-token prediction, imitation learning, language models, comp-stat tradeoffs
